name: Gareth Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six in the farrowing house at Brockley Mill. It's a pig and maize farm, three hundred sows, owned by a farming company with four sites. I check the new litters, look for any piglets that got squashed overnight, then feed, then wash down. Afternoons I'm usually helping on the maize or fixing whatever's broken. Eighteen months ago I was a shift lead in a supermarket warehouse, so I'm very much the new boy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the animals are honest. A sow tells you straight away if something's wrong. What wears me out is the smell in your hair, and that I'm still slow at the stuff the old hands do without thinking, like spotting a piglet that's not getting milk. I take photos and ask the AI on my phone half the time, which makes Kev, the unit manager, roll his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, oh well, it's still a decent tool. I'd keep showing the lads in the break room how I use it to check feed rations and look up pig diseases. Online I'd probably post something like the robot revolution got stuck in traffic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a bit disappointed. I came from a warehouse where robots moved the pallets, and I liked working alongside them. I think farming could use a lot more of that, and a plateau means we stay slow and stubborn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. Learn the job properly, keep using the phone for what it's good at. I'd probably ask Kev if I can trial the sensor collars the feed rep keeps pushing, because even a plateau means some gadgets get cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you liked working alongside robots in the warehouse. What was that like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You stop carrying heavy stuff and start thinking about the flow. My back stopped hurting. But I also saw thirty pickers go in two years, and only six of us were kept as leads. So I know it's not all good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Leah see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leah's a midwife, she thinks I'm a gadget man. She's right. She'd say a plateau's fine, it means fewer people losing work. She keeps me honest.

S0.say: I'd say AI is still a decent tool and keep showing the break room how I check feed rations with it. Online I'd joke that the robot revolution got stuck in traffic.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly. I liked working beside robots in the warehouse and I think farming could use far more of that than it gets.
S0.do: Keeps learning the job and using his phone for feed and disease checks. Asks Kev, the unit manager, to trial the sensor collars a feed rep has been offering.
S0.quote: But I also saw thirty pickers go in two years, and only six of us were kept as leads. So I know it's not all good.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth is an early adopter shaped by a warehouse job where robots arrived alongside him. He's openly disappointed by a world without change. He also remembers thirty pickers losing their jobs, so his enthusiasm has a shadow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if we do it right, meaning the people on the floor get a share. I'd say farms should bring the workers in when they buy kit, not just tell them after. Online I'd probably share stuff about co-ops and worker ownership, which annoys my brother-in-law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well. I'm the one who already asks the phone. If the company puts robot feeders and cameras in, somebody has to set them up and keep them running, and I'd make sure it's me. The bit that bothers me is Kev and the older lads, who'd hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to Kev and offer to run the trial on the automatic feeders and the camera system that counts piglets. I'd do the online course the maker runs, it's about six weeks in the evenings. I'd also keep pushing for a staff rep on the farm, because last time in the warehouse nobody asked us anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Excited, partly. Like the first week at the warehouse when the new system came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the older lads would hate it. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dennis. He's been at Brockley twenty-two years and he can tell a sow's due by the way she makes her nest. If a camera does that, he's lost the thing he's proud of. I'd want him to train the camera, honestly. He knows more than it ever will at the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd spend money on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. We've about a year saved, partly from shares I had in the warehouse company. I might spend a few hundred on a better phone and a course. That's it. I'm not buying a farm.

S1.say: I'd say it's good if done right, with workers getting a share and a say when farms buy new kit. Online I'd share posts about co-ops and worker ownership.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd do well, because I already use AI and someone has to run the robot feeders and cameras. What bothers me is how the older lads would take it.
S1.do: Offers to run the farm's trial of automatic feeders and piglet-counting cameras and takes the maker's six-week evening course. Pushes for a staff rep so workers are consulted on new kit.
S1.feel: Calm and partly excited, like his first week with the warehouse's new system.
S1.quote: If a camera does that, he's lost the thing he's proud of. I'd want him to train the camera, honestly.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change looks like an opportunity to him, and he plans to put himself in charge of the new kit. His progressive side shows in wanting worker reps and in worrying for Dennis, the oldest stockman. His idea that Dennis should train the camera is a striking mix of the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public ownership of some kind, fast. If the machines can do everything in two years, the profit can't just go to whoever owns them. I'd say it everywhere and I'd vote for anyone serious about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my plan of being the robot man only works if the robots need a man. In two years with full AGI, maybe they don't. I've got a year saved and Leah's job, and plenty of farms around, so I'm not scared for this winter. I'm scared for the long run, and for the lads who never touched a phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still volunteer for every new system at Brockley, because being the one who knows it buys me time. I'd put about five thousand of the savings into a fund that holds shares in robot and AI companies, which feels wrong for a lefty but if they're getting all the money I want a slice. And I'd get on to the local party branch, because this is a politics problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicky. More like when you hear a noise in the farrowing house at night and don't know yet what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said buying those shares feels wrong. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my kids need something if wages stop being the way you live. I'd rather argue for sharing it out and own a bit while I argue. Leah would call that hedging. She'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noah and Isla?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noah's thirteen, he already uses AI more than I do. I'd tell him to be the one who asks good questions. Isla's ten, she'd want to know if the pigs would still have someone to scratch their backs.

S2.say: I'd say this needs some kind of public ownership quickly, because the profits can't just go to whoever owns the machines. I'd vote for anyone serious about it.
S2.think: My plan of being the robot man only works if robots still need a man, and in two years they might not. Our savings and Leah's job cover this winter, but I'm scared for the long run.
S2.do: Volunteers for every new system at the farm to buy time. Puts about five thousand of savings into a fund holding AI and robot company shares, and joins the local party branch.
S2.feel: Uneasy, like an unexplained noise in the farrowing house at night.
S2.quote: My plan of being the robot man only works if the robots need a man.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-friendly of his plans hits a wall here, and he says so. He hedges by buying shares in the companies he wants regulated and calls it what it is. His fear is long-term and for others more than for himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the right amount of warning to share the gains properly. Co-ops, worker shares in farms, retraining paid for by a tax on the machines. I'd be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd be properly useful. I'd spend three years being the person who sets up the robots across the company's four sites, and then I'd have a skill to take somewhere when the farm needs nobody. I'd feel ahead rather than behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for a role across all four sites looking after the systems, even if it's a small pay rise. I'd do a proper certificate in farm robotics at the college, they're starting one. On the side I'd help a couple of small farms nearby set up cameras and feeders, paid by the job, to build up my own little business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy. Like I'd have a reason to get up even earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't there a contradiction, pushing for worker protection while helping farms replace workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, there is. I'd tell myself the machines are coming anyway and it's better someone who cares about the lads does the setting up. Maybe that's a story I tell myself. I'd still do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the money side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the year of savings, keep the small fund. If the side business made anything, it'd go into Noah's and Isla's college pot.

S3.say: I'd say five years is the right warning to share the gains properly, through co-ops, worker shares in farms and retraining paid for by a tax on machines.
S3.think: With five years I'd be properly useful, setting up robots across the company's sites and then taking that skill elsewhere. I'd feel ahead instead of behind.
S3.do: Asks for a role looking after systems across the company's four sites and takes the college's new farm robotics certificate. Starts setting up cameras and feeders for small farms nearby, paid by the job.
S3.feel: Calm and busy, with a reason to get up even earlier.
S3.quote: I'd tell myself the machines are coming anyway and it's better someone who cares about the lads does the setting up.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is his sweet spot: enough time to become the expert before the end point. When the contradiction was named, he admitted it might be a story he tells himself. He plans a small side business installing kit for other farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but with ten years I'd say there's time to change the rules properly. I'd want farm workers to own part of the farms that automate, like a share for every job the machines take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'm fifty-three, the mortgage is mostly gone, the kids are grown. I'd probably have had a good run as the robot man. The question I'd ask myself is what I do for the last ten working years, and I think I'd enjoy figuring that out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd be the same as the five-year one: volunteer, take the certificate. I'd not rush the side business, I'd see what the market wants. I'd put a bit into the share fund every year. And I'd talk to Leah about whether she'd train younger midwives, because that feels like the human part that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious. A bit guilty, maybe, that I'm the lucky one in the break room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel guilty. Guilty how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be fine and Dennis wouldn't. He's fifty-eight, he'd retire into nothing. I'd want to make sure there's something for him, a pension top-up, or training young ones on open days. I'd push the company for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time change what you'd tell the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years, Noah could pick a path knowing what's coming. I'd tell him go and learn how these machines think, but also learn to fix things with your hands. Isla, whatever she wants.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves time to change the rules properly, so farm workers own part of the farms that automate, a share for every job a machine takes.
S4.think: At fifty-three, with the mortgage mostly gone and the kids grown, I'd have had a good run as the robot man. I'd enjoy working out what to do with my last working decade.
S4.do: Volunteers for new systems and takes the robotics certificate, holding off on a side business until he sees demand. Adds to the share fund each year and pushes the company for a pension top-up for older staff.
S4.feel: Calm and curious, with some guilt at being the lucky one.
S4.quote: Because I'd be fine and Dennis wouldn't. He's fifty-eight, he'd retire into nothing.
S4.fieldNote: The long timeline mostly feeds his curiosity, and his worry turns towards Dennis. He'd use his position to argue for pension top-ups for older staff. His advice to his son mixes understanding machines with fixing things by hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me so much, we'd cope, but for the lads like Dennis who'd have nothing to hold on to. What would help is a rule that when a farm automates, the workers get a share of what it saves, not just a handshake. And free courses, in the evenings, near home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the animals' side of it. A camera counts piglets, fine, but it doesn't care. I'd want somebody whose job it is to care, even when the machines do everything else. I'd happily be that person.

headlineQuote: A camera counts piglets, fine, but it doesn't care.
portrait: Gareth Torres is 43, a former supermarket warehouse shift lead who has worked for eighteen months in the farrowing house of a company-owned pig and maize farm. He uses AI every day, enjoyed working beside warehouse robots, and plans to make himself the person who runs the farm's new machines. He leans left and wants workers to share in what automation saves, even as he admits he'd help farms automate and would buy shares in AI companies as a hedge. He stays calm across most scenarios, uneasy only when AGI comes in two years, and his worry is mostly for older colleagues like Dennis.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, mostly for older colleagues like Dennis who would have nothing to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A rule giving workers a share of what automation saves a farm, plus free evening courses close to home.
